title: SEASON 4 OPENER: AI Doom and the US v China race
description: Send us Fan Mail Check our Matt & Jimmy' products here: Browzr | Discover the Web Beyond Algorithms Des Cartwright — Paintings Meridian Health Tracker KickoffHQ: Live Start Times & Scores for Every Sport Germanya — Deutsch lernen A senior researcher quits, a “10% chance we all die” quote goes viral, and suddenly the AI safety debate stops sounding like a niche forum argument. We try to make sense of why the mood has changed, and what it means when the people building frontier models talk about catastrophic risk while still racing to release the next system. We dig into concrete failure modes: models that hack, systems that optimise ruthlessly for narrow goals, and the growing push towards recursive self-improvement where AI writes more of its own code and even helps with alignment. We keep it practical and slightly uncomfortable: once humans are no longer the slow part, what does control even look like, especially when everything is connected to the internet and incentives reward capability over caution? Then we put the whole thing through a US China lens. China regulates AI in a more centralised, security-first way, while the US frames the problem as safety and loss of control, but both sides are trapped in a competitive race dynamic. We talk money, IPO pressure, insurance, and the theory that some high-profile safety messaging is also a play for regulation that protects incumbents. Finally, we share our predictions for the next 6 to 18 months, from “useful personal assistant” optimism to jagged cascading degradation: flash crashes, grid outages, poisoned code, and a less open internet. Subscribe for more, share this with the friend who cannot stop arguing about AI doom, and leave a review with your take: should we pause, slow down, or accept the race?
summary: The Season 4 opener tries to make sense of why AI doom suddenly went mainstream: a senior researcher's resignation and a viral '10% chance we all die' quote, endorsed from Musk to Altman to Amodei, landed differently than Hinton's earlier warnings. Matt and Jimmy walk through concrete failure modes — models that hack (Hugging Face), recursive self-improvement loops, agent swarms showing self-preservation-like behavior — before reframing the whole debate through a US-China lens: Beijing regulates for control and sovereignty while Washington talks safety and loss-of-control, and both are trapped in a race dynamic fuelled by IPO pressure and trillions in debt. They close with dueling 6-to-18-month forecasts, from Jimmy's 'useful personal assistant' optimism to Matt's 'jagged cascading degradation' of flash crashes, grid blackouts and Ghost GDP.
keyTalkingPoints: The viral 10% catastrophic-risk quote marks a shift: for the first time the heads of the frontier labs (Musk, Altman, Amodei) publicly agreed with a specific extinction probability, and Trump told everyone not to worry.

RSI (recursive self-improvement) is no longer theoretical: Astra admitted limited use, Gemini 4 rumours point to a stronger self-improvement training loop, and timelines quoted on-air run from Musk's end-2026 to 2027-2028.

China's AI rules are about control, not safety: training data and outputs must reflect 'core socialist values', and Matt argues a frontier model incident in China would be handled inside the system and never made public — he has more faith in that than in US labs protecting their bottom line.

Matt sketches a semi-intentional slowdown thesis: IPO pressure (OpenAI delaying, Anthropic's market sensitivity), insurance, business adoption fatigue and 'seeing things' internally could slow the frontier without anyone agreeing to a pause.

Jimmy floats the 'orchestrated resignation' reading: the safety panic may be partly a play for regulation that protects incumbents — and the Jacob Cox tweet being plastered all over Chinese social media suggests US-China race politics underneath.

Matt coins 'jagged cascading degradation' for the next 6–18 months: an AI-triggered flash crash wiping out $200–500bn, a regional grid blackout for 3–5M customers, then Ghost GDP around 2028 — bad, but not extinction.

jimmy: Most people will take convenience every time — they'll complain about AI slop while consuming it, and robots raising kids will be no different from iPads parenting them today.

He doesn't buy precise doom percentages ('a made up number') but maintains there is no world where superintelligence isn't used for harm; a superintelligent model with bad intentions 'disguises its motives for long enough to get what it wants'.
He suspects some of the safety messaging is strategic: an orchestrated panic that doubles as regulatory moat-building for incumbents, with the China race as cover.
Long term, only one of OpenAI and Anthropic can survive — and he still thinks OpenAI ultimately gets 'swallowed up' like a dot-com casualty.
matt: Self-described doomer who nonetheless doesn't think everyone dies: there will be warning shots, and you'd have to be stupid to walk blindly into extinction — but a rough non-existential future ('another 40% which is pretty shit') is likely.

He partially trusts the market-punishment safety argument but not forever: companies that ship unsafe things will fail, which incentivizes caution — yet that doesn't solve the long-run control problem.

He has more faith in China's centralized system to contain a frontier-model incident than in US labs, because China protects sovereignty and power while US labs protect a bottom line that doesn't exist yet.
He predicts a semi-intentional frontier slowdown driven by IPO math, business adoption lag and internal caution — not a principled pause.
